genres.name: House
genres.summary: Born in Chicago's clubs from disco played on drum machines, house is built on a four-on-the-floor kick and a repetitive groove made for the dancefloor.
genres.description: Straight kick on every quarter, open hi-hat on the off-beat eighths, clap on beats two and four. The foundational gear is the Roland TR-808 and TR-909 plus cheap samplers. Long-loop structure, built for mixing on the console.

tracks.note: Often cited as the first house track pressed to vinyl.
The piano riff that earned it the nickname "The House Music Anthem."

genres.name: Deep House
genres.summary: The warmer, jazzier branch of house, with extended chords, pads and often soulful vocals.
genres.description: Seventh and ninth chords, melodic basslines, restrained tempo. Less about the night's peak moment, more about texture.

tracks.note: Larry Heard brings pads and extended chords into house.

genres.name: Acid House
genres.summary: Defined by a single instrument: the Roland TB-303, used outside its intended purpose to produce squelchy, resonant basslines.
genres.description: The genre's character lies in real-time modulation of the TB-303's cutoff, resonance and accent over a standard house rhythm.

tracks.note: The TB-303 used in a way its maker never intended: a genre born from a misunderstanding.

genres.name: Garage House
genres.summary: The New York strand of house, more vocal and gospel-inflected, tied to the Paradise Garage and Larry Levan.
genres.description: Full vocal takes rather than samples, arrangements close to disco and soul, more live-played production.

genres.name: Tech House
genres.summary: A cross between house's groove and techno's rhythmic severity: minimal sound design, few vocals, bass-focused.
genres.description: Dry percussion, syncopated basslines, arrangements built for the DJ set. The textbook case of a genre with two parents.

genres.name: Latin House
genres.summary: House built on Latin and Caribbean percussion, congas and timbales in place of the drum machine alone.
genres.description: Polyrhythmic percussion patterns, often Spanish-language vocals, strong ties to the New York and Miami scenes.

genres.name: Progressive House
genres.summary: Long-form, progressive house built on extended build-ups rather than the loop.
genres.description: Eight-minute-plus arrangements, gradual layering, wide breakdowns. Born as a British reaction to more direct American house.

genres.name: Afro House
genres.summary: House with percussion and vocals of African origin, strong in South Africa and Angola.
genres.description: Acoustic percussion up front, choral singing, moderate tempo. A bridge between Western house and the scenes of the African continent.

genres.name: Techno
genres.summary: Born in Detroit from the meeting of electronic funk, European synths and post-industrial imagery. Colder and more machinelike than house.
genres.description: Synthetic timbres, near-total absence of vocals, repetition as a compositional principle. Explicit references to Kraftwerk and science fiction.

tracks.note: Formally electro, but Detroit techno's lineage starts here.

genres.name: Minimal Techno
genres.summary: Techno stripped to its essentials: few elements, micro-variations, hypnosis through accumulation.
genres.description: Sound palette reduced to a minimum, almost imperceptible changes spread across long stretches of time.

genres.name: UK Garage
genres.summary: A British reinterpretation of garage house: pitched up, with heavy basslines and chopped vocals.
genres.description: Born from London DJs' practice of playing American garage records sped up. From there it breaks off into an autonomous genre with its own rhythmic rules.

genres.name: Speed Garage
genres.summary: The first wave of UK garage, with reese basslines borrowed from jungle and the kick still on the four.
genres.description: Distorted, modulated bass, dub effects, pitched-up vocal samples.

genres.name: 2-Step
genres.summary: Drops the kick from the second and fourth beat: the result is a limping, syncopated groove that defines the UK sound of the late nineties.
genres.description: Drum patterns without four-to-the-floor, heavy swing, chopped-and-rearranged R&B vocals, clean sub-bass.

tracks.note: 2-step reaches the British pop charts.

genres.name: 4x4 Garage
genres.summary: The branch of UK garage that keeps the straight kick, closer to house than 2-step.
genres.description: Straight groove with the basslines and vocals of the garage vocabulary.

genres.name: Bassline
genres.summary: An evolution of 4x4 garage in the north of England, centered on Sheffield's Niche club.
genres.description: Squared-off, aggressive basslines, fast tempo, strong local identity.

genres.name: UK Funky
genres.summary: A return to a percussive, tribal groove after the grime era, with soca and Afro influences.
genres.description: Percussion up front, tempo around 130, soulful vocals, lighter structure than grime.

genres.name: Breakbeat Hardcore
genres.summary: The British rave sound of the early nineties: sampled breaks, hoover stabs and sped-up vocals.
genres.description: Amen break and other sampled funk breaks, rising tempo, rave aesthetics.

genres.name: Jungle
genres.summary: Amen breaks chopped at extreme speed over reggae basslines and half-time sub-bass.
genres.description: A perceived double speed: drums at 160-170, bass at half time. Jamaican sound system heritage evident in the bass treatment.

genres.name: Drum and Bass
genres.summary: A cleaner, more produced codification of jungle, with greater attention to sound design.
genres.description: More processed, less recognizable breaks, synthesizer-designed bass, structure standardized around two drops.

genres.name: Dubstep
genres.summary: Half-time at 140 BPM, negative space and sub-bass as the main element, born from the darker branch of 2-step.
genres.description: Snare on the third beat, wide empty space between hits, modulated bass occupying the center of the mix.

tracks.note: The track that carries dubstep out of Croydon.

genres.name: Grime
genres.summary: Angular electronic music at 140 BPM built to be rapped over: cheap synthesizers, sparse rhythm, the MC at the center.
genres.description: Often produced on cheap hardware and software, with deliberately digital, cold timbres. Its link to London pirate radio is foundational.

tracks.note: The beat that gives eskibeat its name.

genres.name: Ska
genres.summary: The first modern popular Jamaican genre: guitar offbeats, horns and fast tempo.
genres.description: Accent on the upstroke of guitar and piano, prominent horn section, mento and American rhythm and blues influences.

genres.name: Rocksteady
genres.summary: A slowdown of ska, with the bass promoted to lead melodic instrument.
genres.description: Fewer horns, more harmonized vocals, basslines written as independent melodies.

genres.name: Reggae
genres.summary: An offbeat groove with the accent on the third beat (one drop) and deep bass; nearly all subsequent Jamaican music passes through here.
genres.description: Guitar skank on the off-beats, one-drop pattern on the drums, full, repetitive bass.

tracks.note: The first recording to use the word in its title.

genres.name: Dub
genres.summary: The remix before the remix: strip out the vocal and treat drums and bass with delay and reverb, turning the mixing desk into an instrument.
genres.description: A studio practice more than a genre of songwriting: drop-outs, tape echoes, spring reverbs, instrumental versions on the B-side.

genres.name: Dancehall
genres.summary: Electronic riddims and the deejay up front; since the eighties it has been the center of gravity of Jamaican music.
genres.description: Riddims reused by multiple artists as a shared backing track, digital production from 1985 onward, deejay-style vocals.

genres.name: Kwaito
genres.summary: House slowed to a walking pace with spoken vocals in township slang, the soundtrack of post-apartheid South Africa.
genres.description: Imported house slowed to around 100 BPM, lyrics in isiZulu, Sesotho and tsotsitaal.

genres.name: Amapiano
genres.summary: A South African sound built around the log drum, with jazzy pads, slow tempo and long hypnotic structures.
genres.description: The log drum is a synthesized percussive bass that serves as both bassline and rhythmic element. Long tracks, constant shakers, deep-house piano chords.

genres.name: Gqom
genres.summary: Born in Durban: broken, raw rhythm, no straight kick, dark, minimal percussion.
genres.description: Triplet patterns and broken grooves, deliberately raw production, heavy use of percussion and empty space.

genres.name: Afrobeat
genres.summary: Fela Kuti's genre: highlife, jazz and funk in long, political tracks. Not to be confused with the plural afrobeats.
genres.description: Ten- to twenty-minute tracks, large horn section, polyrhythmic groove, politically critical lyrics.

genres.name: Afrobeats
genres.summary: West African pop of the 2000s, blending highlife, dancehall and digital production. An umbrella term, not a direct descendant of afrobeat.
genres.description: A commercial label born in the London diaspora to group together very different Nigerian and Ghanaian productions.

genres.name: Rhythm and Blues
genres.summary: The postwar African American strand that fuses blues, jazz and gospel into dance songs for a Black urban audience: the harmonic and vocal foundation from which soul, funk and, later, hip hop descend.
genres.description: Rhythm section marked on the backbeat (two and four), twelve-bar blues forms or pop song structures, vocals often of gospel origin with call-and-response phrasing, combos with horns and piano. It emerges as a commercial category replacing the racist label "race records" and soon becomes an autonomous idiom.

tracks.note: In Roy Brown's version (1947), among the first records to embody the new sound renamed rhythm and blues.
Big Mama Thornton brings blues groove and attitude into the R&B song form.

genres.name: Funk
genres.summary: James Brown strips the beat down to the chord: the guitar becomes percussion, the bass dictates the syncopation, and the groove is built on the first beat of every bar, "the one."
genres.description: A hard downbeat ("on the one"), percussive chicken-scratch guitars, stabbing horns, syncopated basslines often slapped. Open forms built on a repeated vamp rather than complex harmonic progressions.

tracks.note: James Brown reduces the harmony to a vamp and shifts the center to rhythmic groove: funk is born.

genres.name: Hip Hop
genres.summary: Born at Bronx block parties as a DJ practice — isolating and looping the instrumental break of funk and soul records — it soon becomes a voice too: MCs talking rhythmically over the beat.
genres.description: Four founding elements: DJing (breakbeats, scratching), MCing (rapping), breaking (dance), graffiti. Musically it begins with sampling and looping the percussive break of funk, soul and disco records, then with beats built from scratch on drum machines.

tracks.note: The first commercial rap hit, built on a loop of Chic's "Good Times."
Grandmaster Flash carries rap out of the party and into social commentary.

genres.name: Trap
genres.summary: The 2000s sound of Atlanta telling the story of the "trap," the house where drugs are sold: hammering 808s, hi-hats arpeggiated in thirty-second notes, dark horror-soundtrack atmospheres.
genres.description: Kick and 808 sub often pitched to tune the bassline, hi-hats with fast rolls and triplets, snare on the off-beat, minor-key synths and Middle-Eastern-tinged bells. Lyrics centered on street economics.

tracks.note: Gucci Mane's debut album, which gives the genre its name and imagery.

genres.name: Drill
genres.summary: A dark, menacing offshoot of trap born on Chicago's South Side: crushing 808s, syncopated and irregular rhythms, raw street-reportage lyrics.
genres.description: Slow, dragging tempo despite frantic hi-hats, sliding 808 basslines, industrial synths. Tightly linked to the "drill on YouTube" phenomenon and diss tracks between rival crews.

tracks.note: Chief Keef brings Chicago drill to national attention.

genres.name: UK Drill
genres.summary: Chicago drill transplanted to London hybridizes with grime's rhythmic backbone and takes on a thoroughly British accent, made of local slang and sliding basslines.
genres.description: It inherits sliding 808s and stretched-out tempo from American drill, but grafts on hi-hat patterns and syncopated groove close to grime; production is often handled by specialized producer teams.

genres.name: Rage
genres.summary: Trap taken to the extreme: distorted, saturated synths, hi-hats that sound like glitches, mosh-pit energy closer to punk than to traditional rap.
genres.description: Dense, saturated productions, often using free synthesis plugins pushed past their limits, distorted kick and 808s, structure built for live performance and crowd surfing.

tracks.note: Playboi Carti sets the saturated, chaotic aesthetic of rage.

genres.name: G-Funk
genres.summary: Dr. Dre dresses West Coast gangsta rap in whining synths, live-played funk basslines and Parliament-Funkadelic samples: the sound of Los Angeles in the early nineties.
genres.description: Whiny lead synths, often Moog, played or re-created funk basslines, heavy sampling of the P-Funk catalog, relaxed tempo, production more lush than the contemporaneous East Coast boom-bap.

tracks.note: Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg set the G-funk sound on a mainstream scale.

genres.name: Miami Bass
genres.summary: Electro pushed to subwoofer extremes: hammering 808s, fast tempo and call-and-response hooks built for Miami's tricked-out car stereos.
genres.description: 808-driven backing with heavy kick and toms, fast tempo, often explicit vocal samples, strong ties to trunk-rattling car audio culture and volume competitions.

tracks.note: Afrika Bambaataa's electro-funk template that inspires the Miami sound.
2 Live Crew sets the explicit tone and 808 beat of Miami bass.

genres.name: Funk Carioca
genres.summary: Miami bass imported into Rio's favelas becomes the soundtrack of the baile: 808s reworked with a local twist, MCs improvising over instrumentals shared across the whole scene.
genres.description: 808 basslines often built on the "tamborzão," an electronic percussion pattern shared by hundreds of producers as a common backing track (similar to Jamaican riddims), rhythmic vocals close to rap, tempo built for dancing on the floor.

tracks.note: The tamborzão becomes recognizable internationally.

genres.name: Brega
genres.summary: Romantic, melodramatic pop from the North of Brazil, long dismissed as "tacky" by the cultural elites of the South and later reclaimed with pride by the periphery.
genres.description: Sentimental melodies, cheap pop orchestrations, emphatic and expressive vocals; the term (literally "tacky") starts as a class insult and is later reappropriated by the scene itself.

genres.name: Brega Funk
genres.summary: The meeting of brega's melodic sentimentality with funk carioca's electronic beat, born in Recife and turned into a viral dance phenomenon thanks to the "passinho."
genres.description: Funk carioca basslines reinterpreted with brega melodies and synths, tempo slightly more restrained than funk carioca, a strong choreographic component built for social media.
